en.title: Leisure and activities
en.goal: Talk about hobbies and make weekend plans.

lessons.cantar-fim-de-semana-sair-filme: Singing, the weekend, going out and the movie

vocab: to play (a game) / to play (an instrument)

phrases.t: What do you do on the weekend?
phrases.scenario: You want to know what a friend usually does on weekends. What do you ask?
Someone asks what your favorite hobby is, and it's reading books. What do you say?

phrases.t: Shall we go to the movies tonight?
phrases.scenario: You want to invite a friend to the movies tonight. What do you ask?
Someone asks what your brother can do — he plays the guitar. What do you answer?

phrases.t: The movie theater is closed tonight.
Sports are good for your health.
We're going out on Saturday night.
The movie starts at eight o'clock.

dialogue.title: The weekend
lines: Do you have any plans for the weekend?
Yes, I'm going to the movies with friends.
Which movie are you going to see?

jouer-de-vs-jouer-a.title: "Jouer DE la guitare" or "jouer AU foot"?
jouer-de-vs-jouer-a.body: For musical instruments, use jouer de: jouer de la guitare, jouer du piano. For sports and games, use jouer à: jouer au foot, jouer aux cartes. It's a simple little rule, but without it you can mix everything up — worth memorizing this pair of prepositions.
examples: to play (a game) / to play (an instrument)

cinema-nasceu-na-franca.title: Cinema was born in France
cinema-nasceu-na-franca.body: In 1895, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière held in Paris the first public, paid screening of films in history, using the cinematograph they had invented themselves. That's why France is considered the birthplace of cinema — and it still has a highly valued film scene today, with the Cannes Film Festival among the most important in the world.

ne-drop-on-sait-pas.title: In everyday speech, "On ne sait pas encore !" loses its "ne"
ne-drop-on-sait-pas.body: In everyday speech, the ne of the negation almost always disappears — on sait pas encore instead of "on ne sait pas encore". It's probably the most common simplification in all of spoken French, and it applies to any "ne... pas" negation. In the exercises here, keep writing the "ne" — it's the form the exercises ask for.

trueFalse.claim: This is a way of inviting someone out.
trueFalse.whyNote: Correct — on va...? is a casual way of suggesting plans, like "shall we go to the movies tonight?".

review.en: to play (a game) / to play (an instrument)
review.why: English uses 'play' for both; the French distinction (jouer à / jouer de) is the lesson point, kept in the concept note.

review.pt: A gente vai ao cinema hoje à noite?
review.en: Shall we go to the movies tonight?
review.why: 'on' = informal 'we'; 'Are we going to the movies tonight?' is the literal alternative. 'Shall we' is more of a suggestion, chosen for the invitation sense.

review.pt: As crianças gostam de brincar lá fora.
review.why: 'Les enfants' generic; 'The children like...' also possible.

review.pt: Vamos sair no sábado à noite.
review.en: We're going out on Saturday night.
review.why: 'On va sortir' = informal near future; 'Let's go out' is a possible reading but PT says 'Vamos sair' as statement.

review.pt: O filme começa às vinte horas.
review.en: The movie starts at eight o'clock.
review.why: French 24-hour 'vingt heures' = 8 PM; English would say 8 p.m. Kept 'eight o'clock' (PM implied). Could be '8 p.m.'.

review.pt: O cinema está fechado hoje à noite.
review.en: The movie theater is closed tonight.

review.why: Cultural note translated faithfully; 'birthplace of cinema' wording follows PT.
Reality note; 'a gente' = informal 'we' lost in English.

review.pt: Essa é uma forma de convidar alguém pra sair.
review.en: This is a way of inviting someone out.
review.why: 'pra sair' = to go out/hang out; 'inviting someone out' natural.
